title: From India U19 to Team USA: Saurabh Netravalkar's Unlikely Cricket Journey
excerpt: A Mumbai boy who gave up professional cricket for a Cornell engineering degree rebuilt his career on weekend club games in California — and became the face of America's rise at the 2024 T20 World Cup.
body:
• Saurabh Netravalkar — the left-arm pacer who bowled the USA to its famous 2024 T20 World Cup Super Over win over Pakistan — began his career with Mumbai's age-group sides and India's U19 team at the 2010 World Cup.
  • After a single Ranji Trophy appearance for Mumbai, he walked away from full-time cricket in 2015, earned a master's in computer science at Cornell, and joined Oracle as an engineer in California.
  • Weekend club cricket rebuilt his career: he played 50-over games in Los Angeles and San Francisco around his work week, debuted for the USA in 2019, captained the side, and became the first American bowler to 100 ODI wickets.
  • The latest chapter of his story is a new Times of India "Diaspora Dialogues" interview with Sujatha Padmanabhan, on balancing an Oracle engineering job with international cricket, identity, and the future of cricket in America.

Saurabh Netravalkar has lived two sporting lives. In the first, he was a Mumbai schoolboy quick who climbed through the Under-13, Under-15 and Under-17 ranks, represented India at the 2010 Under-19 World Cup and made a single Ranji Trophy appearance for Mumbai. In the second, he is the left-arm pacer who defended 18 runs in a Super Over against Pakistan and dismissed Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli in the same match — wearing the colours of the United States, while holding down a full-time software engineering job at Oracle.

That bridge is the subject of a new "Diaspora Dialogues" episode from the Times of India, in which Netravalkar joins host Sujatha Padmanabhan to unpack the journey behind his rise.

Context & Background

Born in Mumbai in 1991, Netravalkar grew up playing street cricket in Malad, imitating left-arm quicks like Wasim Akram and Zaheer Khan. He was India's new-ball bowler at the 2010 U19 World Cup in New Zealand — England's Joe Root among his scalps — and shared Mumbai dressing rooms with Suryakumar Yadav, a close friend since their Under-15 days.

https://x.com/WSHFreedom/status/2108104742123475104

But the step up never came. After two years of full-time cricket yielded just one Ranji Trophy game for Mumbai, he made the call that defines his story: he quit, moved to the United States in 2015 for a master's at Cornell, and joined Oracle in California. "I gave two years full time to cricket but felt I wasn't making it to the next level," he told the Times of India. A local club near his workplace pulled him back in, and his second act was built on weekend 50-over games in Los Angeles and San Francisco fitted around his work week. In January 2018 he became eligible for USA selection; later that year he captained the side at the ICC World Cricket League Division Three in Oman, and in April 2019 he led the team to ODI status.

Impact & Analysis

The 2024 T20 World Cup turned Netravalkar from a curiosity into a headline. His nerveless Super Over against Pakistan sealed one of the great upsets in tournament history, and days later he took 2 for 18 against India — removing Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli — as the USA reached the Super 8s on debut. He finished with six wickets at 20.83, then topped the Major League Cricket bowling charts with 15 wickets as Washington Freedom won the title. In 2025 he became the first USA bowler to claim 100 ODI wickets.

The one door that stayed shut was the IPL — despite being shortlisted, he went unsold at the 2025 mega auction at a base price of ₹30 lakh. "Yes, the child in me had hopes for sure," he told the Times of India, adding that the quality of the player pool made the outcome understandable — and that he would keep working to come back stronger next year.

Diaspora Angle

Netravalkar's story is the Indian-American experience in miniature: the pressure to choose the safe profession, the identity stretched across two flags, and the refusal to pick just one. In the conversation he discusses growing up between Indian and American cultures, what it means to play for Team USA, and how Oracle accommodated the double life — the company's gym became his training ground, and colleagues cheered him on through the World Cup.

There is a full-circle thread, too. At a 2009 National Cricket Academy camp, a young Netravalkar bowled to Rahul Dravid; more than a decade later, with Dravid as India's head coach, the two met again during the World Cup — and Dravid remembered him and appreciated the Pakistan performance.

What's Next

At 34, Netravalkar remains the spearhead of an American side with a genuine runway: Major League Cricket is expanding, and cricket returns to the Olympics at Los Angeles 2028 — a home Games for a team built on stories like his.

nri_angle: Netravalkar's journey — from Mumbai's age-group cricket to a Cornell engineering degree and an Oracle career in California to starring for Team USA — captures the Indian-American experience of carrying two identities, and he has become one of the faces of cricket's growth in the United States.
